{{Short description|American mathematician}}
{{other people|Thomas Wolf}}
[[File:Thomas Wolff.jpg|thumb|Wolff in 1992]]
'''Thomas Hartwig Wolff''' (July 14, 1954, [[New York City]] &ndash; July 31, 2000, [[Kern County]]) was an American mathematician, working primarily in the fields of [[harmonic analysis]], [[complex analysis]], and [[partial differential equation]]s.  As an undergraduate at [[Harvard University]], he regularly played poker with his classmate [[Bill Gates]].  While a graduate student at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] from 1976 to 1979, under the direction of [[Donald Sarason]], he obtained a new proof of the [[corona theorem]], a famously difficult theorem in [[complex analysis]].  He was made Professor of Mathematics at [[Caltech]] in 1986, and was there from 1988–1992 and from 1995 to his death in a car accident in 2000.  He also held positions at the [[University of Washington]], [[University of Chicago]], [[New York University]], and [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Chang |first=Kenneth |date=August 10, 2000 |title=Thomas Wolff, Math Expert, Dies at 46 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/08/10/us/thomas-wolff-math-expert-dies-at-46.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=July 19, 2019 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.math.caltech.edu/wolffobit.html |title=Thomas Wolff  |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=Caltech Department of Mathematics |publisher=California Institute of Technology |access-date=July 19, 2019 }}</ref>

He received the [[Salem Prize]] in 1985 and the [[Bôcher Memorial Prize]] in 1999, for his contributions to analysis and particularly to the [[Kakeya conjecture]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ams.org/notices/199904/comm-bocher-prz.pdf |title=1999 Bocher Prize |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=April 1999 |website=Notices of the AMS |publisher=American Mathematical Society |access-date=July 19, 2019 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Simon |first1=Barry |author-link=Barry Simon |last2=Carleson |first2=Lennart |author-link2=Lennart Carleson |date=May 2001 |title=Thomas H. Wolff (1954–2000) |url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200105/fea-wolff.pdf |journal=Notices of the AMS |volume=48 |issue=5 |pages=482–490 |access-date=July 19, 2019 }}</ref> He was an Invited Speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in 1986 in Berkeley<ref>{{cite book|author=Wolff, T. H.|chapter=Generalizations of Fatou’s theorem|title=Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians, Berkeley, CA|volume=2|pages=990–993|year=1986}}</ref> and in 1998 in Berlin.<ref>{{cite book|author=Wolff, Thomas|chapter=Maximal averages and packing of one dimensional sets|title=Doc. Math. (Bielefeld) Extra Vol. ICM Berlin, 1998, vol. II|year=1998|pages=755–761|chapter-url=https://www.elibm.org/ft/10011687000}}</ref>
